cells.tense: You are here with the pen, and the telling-apart is clean right now.
cells.ask: Name one distinction you drew this week and what it settled, out loud to someone.
cells.core:
You can sit with a question that isn't finished. Half-lit situations don't rattle you into forcing them into something tidier, and you keep telling apart what counts from what doesn't as you go.

That pairing is working: the careful eye and the room for things to stay open. When the ground was fog you took the next step anyway instead of reaching for a full picture to hide inside. Keep at it past where it feels done. Write down one distinction you've been carrying as a hunch, and let the page keep the next step clear and the road ahead unclear. That's the work. It holds, and it costs a bit: the light stays dim longer than you'd like some weeks.

cells.tense: You are bracing for a call you'll have to defend before it arrives.
cells.ask: Say one uncertain thing and stop — no follow-up, no pressure to make the other person agree.
cells.core:
The distinguishing has moved ahead of you. A live question gets scanned for what could go wrong, worked over before it's asked, and the analysis you bring is sharper than the moment warrants. You're trying to get far enough ahead of the ambiguity that it can't touch you.

It doesn't work that way. The next step clears when you take it, not when you've mapped the ways it could fail. What helps is a place to put the effort — an outcome you can see is worth the weight. So try it on one open question: say your read, then stop. No pre-empting, no three-deep contingency. Let the answer sit overnight. Nothing about you is settled by whether you solve it tonight.

cells.tense: The careful distinguishing has been quiet a while, and you're still walking as though it spoke this morning.
cells.ask: Answer one question you usually put off, and take a step from it today instead of re-deciding later.
cells.core:
Telling apart what counts from what doesn't has gone quiet. You meet an open question now by waiting for it to settle itself, or by handing it to someone else to answer. Keeping a thing open is easier than sorting it and finding out what you actually think.

That's a thin way to live, and it wears on whatever the choice touches. Give the distinguishing something small and live — one question somebody is waiting on you for — and give an answer, rough is fine. You'll get something back either way: a clean yes or a fixable no. Both are easier to hold than a package left unopened. It stays your call, too. Nobody else has to decide this one for you.

cells.tense: The careful distinguishing is running — you're doing it now — and you talk about it like borrowed weather.
cells.ask: Say one of those half-conscious distinctions out loud, to one person, and keep it yours.
cells.core:
You can tell which option is real and which is noise, which plan will hold and which one is stalling, and you don't argue about it. You call that staying open.

Nothing there is actually undecided. The distinction got drawn in the moment, and the moment passed. What's missing is the sentence that says so. Tell one person what you can see about a thing you're calling not-yet-a-decision — not the case for it, just the fact of it. That doesn't force a door shut, and it doesn't harden anything. It hands the drawing back to the one who's been making it the whole time.
